objection: Was Jesus made God at the Council of Nicaea?
answer:
Let me take the historical claim seriously, because it's the right question to ask, and then push back on where the evidence actually points.

You're right that Nicaea produced a technical term — homoousios — that no apostle wrote. But the material we have shows the council wasn't manufacturing worship of Jesus as God; it was fencing worship that already existed. The confession that Jesus is Lord is not a fourth-century deposit but is embedded in the oldest strata of the New Testament itself — hymnic and creedal material predating Paul's letters. Paul doesn't argue for Jesus' divine status as a novelty; he assumes it as shared ground with his readers, decades before any Arian controversy existed. Colossians 1:15–20 already places Christ on the Creator side of the Creator-creature line — "firstborn of all creation" glossed immediately by "by him were all things created" — which is not the language of "God exalted a man," but of eternal agency in creation itself. Matthew 28:19 and 2 Corinthians 13:14 show a triadic liturgical pattern — one name shared by Father, Son, and Spirit — already fixed before any council existed to legislate it.

So the fourth-century fight wasn't earliest Christians disagreeing about whether Jesus was divine; it was a fight over how to say what "divine" meant in the face of Arius's specific claim that the Son, though highest of creatures, was made — "there was when He was not." That's a technical dispute about the metaphysics of an already-confessed divinity, not evidence the confession itself was up for grabs. Disagreement about how best to articulate a truth doesn't prove the truth was invented in the argument — Christians had disputed how to read Scripture on other questions for centuries without anyone concluding the text was blank until the dispute was settled. Nicaea's vote was overwhelming, not a coin-flip Constantine tipped; it canonized what Ignatius and the Philippian hymn had already confessed. I'd concede this: the philosophical vocabulary (ousia, hypostasis) is genuinely fourth-century achievement, sharpening ambiguity in Greek metaphysical categories. But that's development of expression, not amplification of substance — and the material here doesn't give me grounds to trace Arius's own theological genealogy further than that, so I'll leave that historical question where the evidence stops.
